title: Females Choose the Longer Sword
quote: Females prefer males with the longest swords as mates [13]. ... Still, we do not believe that the sword is cost-free altogether. Basolo and Alcaraz [15] demonstrated that the sword increases the energetic cost of both steady and courtship swimming.
newFact: A male swordtail's namesake sword is no free accessory. Research shows the long tail extension makes swimming cost more energy, both for everyday cruising and for courtship displays. Females still prefer males with the longest swords as mates, so the flashiest guys haul their pricey ornament around anyway.
note: Replaced 'no role in swimming, pure ornament' with the energy cost of swimming; dropped the 1990 study gap-strength line (Basolo 1990 abstract unreachable: Crossref has no abstract, ScienceDirect 403).

title: The Fish Behind GloFish
quote: Almost 20 years after NUS Biological Sciences Professor Gong Zhiyuan first inserted a fluorescent jellyfish gene into zebrafish ... Prof Gong ... wanted to develop zebrafish that look just like its ordinary black-and-silver striped peers, but would glow in response to toxins in the waters as a means to detect and fight environmental pollution. ... Texas-based Yorktown Technologies soon came knocking on Prof Gong's door and a licensing deal was struck for the use of NUS' technology to create their proprietary GloFish. The first fluorescent zebrafish marketed was red, which incorporated a bright red gene from the sea anemone.
newFact: GloFish started out as a pollution alarm. Professor Gong Zhiyuan at the National University of Singapore put a fluorescent jellyfish gene into zebra danios, aiming for fish that would glow in response to toxins in the water. A US company licensed the idea, and the first GloFish sold was red, borrowing its glow from a sea anemone gene.
note: Jellyfish gene now tied to Gong's original lab fish; the first GloFish sold used a red sea anemone gene. Nothing dropped.

title: Not Actually Whiskers
quote: Snout tentacles appear to be modifications of the fleshy cutaneous sheath that surrounds the base of an odontode (integumentary tooth) and are best developed in breeding males. The tentacles are thought to serve as accessory sensory structures because they are covered with taste buds. ... We hypothesize that female Ancistrus preferentially spawn with males guarding larvae, and that the male's snout tentacles stimulate this bias by mimicking the presence of larvae in an otherwise empty nest.
newFact: Those branching "bristles" on a male bristlenose pleco aren't whiskers. They're fleshy tentacles growing from the skin around tiny tooth-like odontodes, and they're covered in taste buds. Scientists have a cheeky theory for why breeding males sport the biggest ones: the tentacles may mimic baby fish, fooling females into thinking his nest already holds a brood.
note: Bristles are fleshy tentacles from the sheath around an odontode, not odontodes; dropped gill covers of both sexes, sparring (cheek spines do that) and breeding-readiness signal; added the same paper's larval mimicry hypothesis.

title: Eating Poop for the B12
quote: Mean frequency of coprophagy per animal per day was 9.6 when animals were fed on the basal diet, whereas the frequency was immediately and significantly (p<0.05-p<0.01) reduced to 4.7 after the diet had been replaced by the fortified one. Furthermore, under the fortified diet, the frequency of coprophagy increased gradually. ... This indicates that some nutrient (s) in feces other than vitamin B 12 might be of use to the host, and that otherwise, coprophagy might be a basically habitual form of behavior.
newFact: Mice eat their own droppings, and vitamin B12 is part of the draw. In a 1986 study, mice on a standard diet did it about 9.6 times a day, a rate that fell right away to 4.7 once their food was fortified with B12. Then the snacking slowly crept back up, so plain habit may play a part too.
note: Replaced 'direct evidence of nutritional demand rather than instinct' with the paper's finding that the rate crept back up and may be partly habitual. Nothing else dropped.

title: Musking Takes Real Energy
newTitle: Snakes in Good Shape Stink More
quote: In this study we quantify musking behaviors in the Terrestrial Gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans) and the Plains Gartersnake (T. radix) when hand-captured at four sites in and near Denver, Colorado, USA. ... Additionally, we observed a positive correlation in body condition and musking propensity in Terrestrial Gartersnakes, suggesting resource-dependent behavior in this species.
newFact: A garter snake's stinky musk defense may depend on how well stocked the snake is. When researchers caught two garter snake species by hand near Denver, terrestrial garter snakes in better body condition were more likely to musk. The team says that suggests the smelly defense depends on the snake's resources.
note: Narrowed 'wild garter snakes' to terrestrial garter snakes; dropped 'spray', 'genuinely costs the snake' and 'not just a panic reflex'; title changed since energy cost is not shown.

title: Killer Whale Family Trees
quote: Resident killer whales live in stable social groups that are organized along maternal lines. ... Dispersal of juveniles and adults from these groups appears to be absent in the resident communities (Bigg et al. 1990). ... Ford (1989, 1991) showed that groups of related matrilines called pods have unique vocal repertoires of 7-17 discrete call types ... he detected no differences in the call types used by certain groups over a 30-year period.
newFact: Resident killer whales live in family groups built along their mothers' lines, and neither youngsters nor adults seem to leave. Each pod has its own dialect of 7 to 17 distinct call types, and one researcher found no change in the call types some groups used over 30 years. That's a family accent kept for decades.
note: 'Clicks and whistles' became discrete call types; dropped matriarch leadership and 'calves spend years learning' (not in source, and a second point).

title: The Biggest Nest in the Tree
quote: Bald eagles build some of the largest of all bird nests, typically 5 to 6 feet in diameter and 2 to 4 feet tall ... Nests can take up to three months to build, and may be reused (and added to) year after year. ... The largest bald eagle nest on record, in St. Petersburg, Florida, was 10 feet in diameter and 20 feet tall. Another famous nest, in Vermilion, Ohio, was shaped like a wine glass and weighed over 2 tons. It was used for 34 years until the tree blew down.
newFact: A bald eagle pair may reuse and add to the same nest year after year, so a nest that usually starts 5 to 6 feet across just keeps growing. The record, in St. Petersburg, Florida, was 10 feet across and 20 feet tall. A wine glass shaped one in Vermilion, Ohio, topped 2 tons over 34 years of use.
note: '20 feet deep' became 20 feet tall; dropped 'nothing else in North America builds a bigger nest' (NPS says only 'some of the largest'), so title changed. NPS gives 10 feet; USFWS and Guinness say 9.5.

title: It Dives in a Curve on Purpose
quote: The line of sight of the deep fovea points forwards and approximately 45 degrees to the right or left of the head axis ... The anatomy of the foveae suggests that the deep fovea has the higher acuity. Several species of raptors in this study repeatedly moved their heads among three positions while looking at an object: straight ... or sideways to the right or left ... The movements occurred approximately every 2 s on average in hawks and falcons, and approximately every 5 s in bald eagles. ... At distances of 40 m or more, raptors looked sideways at the object 80 % or more of the time.
newFact: A bald eagle's sharpest vision doesn't point straight ahead. Each eye has two foveae, and the deep one, thought to be the sharpest, aims about 45 degrees to the side. In tests, bald eagles switched between looking straight and turning their heads sideways about every 5 seconds, and raptors studying faraway objects mostly looked sideways.
note: Curved dive dropped (modeled for an 'ideal falcon', seen in peregrines, not eagles); rebuilt on the same abstract's bald eagle head-turning data; dropped 'single fovea humans have'.

title: Six Toed Cliff Climber
quote: The Lundehund has six fully developed toes on each foot. ... The extra toes provide more traction and grip when the dog is navigating the steep or slippery rocks and peaks of his Norwegian homeland. ... he is capable of touching the top of his head to his back, which enables him to turn around while inside a narrow underground passageway. The Lundehund also has an extremely flexible shoulder joint, allowing him to spread his forelegs out to the sides.
newFact: The Norwegian Lundehund has six fully developed toes on each foot, a shoulder joint so flexible its front legs spread out to the sides, and a neck that bends until the top of its head touches its back. Bred to hunt puffins, it uses that kit for grip on slippery rock and for turning around in narrow passages.
note: 'Extra joints in its shoulders' became one extremely flexible shoulder joint; dropped 'neck vertebrae' and 'at least'.
